claims.text: Superior wear resistance of HEA coatings is primarily governed by dynamic strain hardening.
High configurational entropy enables the dynamic strain-hardening mechanism.
The full-entropy state stabilizes a nanoscale multiphase microstructure.
A fine multiphase microstructure provides grain and phase boundaries that impede dislocation motion and deformation transfer during wear.
Interactions between dislocations and hard phases or nanoprecipitates increase dislocation storage and work hardening in the worn subsurface.
Reducing the number of principal elements lowers configurational entropy.
Reducing configurational entropy interferes with wear-induced local chemical or phase segregation and nanoscale structural evolution.
Reduced configurational entropy diminishes dynamic strain hardening.
At comparable bulk hardness and under identical wear conditions, reduced-entropy coatings will develop lower dislocation density or fewer dislocation barriers than full-entropy coatings.
At comparable bulk hardness and under identical wear conditions, reduced-entropy coatings will have higher wear rates and more severe wear tracks than full-entropy coatings.
High sliding-induced deformation and stress can activate dislocation-mediated hardening mechanisms in heterogeneous HEA microstructures.
The proposed entropy-controlled mechanism should hold under moderate-to-high loads and sliding speeds when plastic deformation dominates wear.
Oxide films can reduce wear by limiting direct contact and can also increase surface hardness.
When oxidation-related wear protection predominates, it may mask the contribution of dynamic strain hardening.
